1b9b8d59bd: This chapter is about trust. Tests give you a reason to trust your own code. Concurrency lets one program do more at once, but only if you pick the right tool for the kind of work. And a few safety habits keep small programs from becoming security holes. These three topics sit together because they all answer the same question: will this code behave when it matters?
97aa22abd8: Two more terms before the example. A fixture is the known starting state a test needs. Here, that's a fresh bank account with 100 in it. setUp builds the fixture before every test method, and tearDown cleans up after. Each test gets its own fixture, so tests cannot pollute each other.
a1ce729c94: A realistic note on placement. In a real project the BankAccount class would live in its own module (say bank.py), and the test file would import it. Keeping both in one file here is a teaching shortcut, so the example runs as-is.
cfcb04c474: The most common unittest mistake is a test that never runs. If the method name does not start with test, the runner silently skips it. The symptom is unmistakable once you know it. The summary says Ran 0 tests and everything is "OK," because nothing ran. Always glance at the test count.
7e607d1ae8: When do you not need unittest? For a ten-line throwaway script, a quick REPL check is fine. The moment code gets reused, imported, or edited more than once, tests pay for themselves. For tiny checks there's a simpler alternative: plain assert statements in a scratch script. They are not a test suite, but they beat eyeballing.
669750950c: Happy-path tests check that correct input gives correct output. The bugs live at the edges: zero, empty, negative, one-too-many. And sometimes the exception is the behavior. A function that should reject bad input is only correct if it actually rejects it.
16dd22ca0a: unittest checks expected exceptions with assertRaises. You saw the callable form in the last example. The more flexible form is a context manager. The code inside the with block must raise, and you get the exception object back to inspect.
b45290a0b0:
A few things are worth noticing.

  • The boundary tests (0% and 100%) probe exactly where the allowed range ends. Off-by-one errors love boundaries.
  • assertAlmostEqual compares floats with a tolerance, because 0.1 + 0.2 style arithmetic rarely lands exactly.
  • ctx.exception lets you check the message, not just the type. Otherwise a ValueError raised for the wrong reason would pass your test.
d1654c5e6c: The classic assertRaises mistake is writing self.assertRaises(ValueError, apply_discount(-5.0, 10)). That calls the function immediately. The exception fires before assertRaises ever runs, and your test errors instead of passing. Pass the callable and its arguments separately, or use the with form. The with form is easier to read, and it's the one you will reach for most.
ca2f484695: So when should you test exceptions? Test the errors your callers depend on. If your function's contract says "raises ValueError on bad input," that contract deserves a test. Do not test that Python itself raises TypeError when someone passes a string where you do arithmetic. That is Python's behavior, not yours.
405e70dea1: pytest.approx is pytest's answer to assertAlmostEqual: float comparison with tolerance. The match="negative" argument checks the exception message with a regex, like inspecting ctx.exception in unittest.
988043a839:
Reach for pytest in any real project where you control the environment. Its failure output alone is worth the install. Stay with unittest in locked-down environments where you cannot install packages, or in codebases already written in unittest style. The two can coexist in one repo, but pick one per project.

Learning unittest first is the right order. It teaches the concepts (cases, fixtures, assertions) that pytest then makes more convenient.
4e608bfd39:
Threads share one process and one memory space. The catch is the GIL, the Global Interpreter Lock. It means only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time.

That sounds like threads are useless. But the GIL is released while a thread waits, whether on a network response, on disk, or on a lock. So threads shine for I/O-bound work. Ten threads downloading files genuinely overlap, because each spends most of its life waiting with the GIL released.
9d23a741f7: One version note, scoped carefully. Python 3.13 added experimental support for running without the GIL. These "free-threaded" builds are usually invoked as python3.13t (see What's New in Python 3.13, PEP 703). The feature is experimental and not the default. The standard python3.13 you installed keeps the GIL, and everything in this chapter assumes that.
6c9274c5a9:
Processes (the multiprocessing module) sidestep the GIL completely. Each process is its own Python interpreter with its own memory and its own GIL, so they truly run in parallel on multiple cores.

The price is real. Processes are heavy to start, they cannot share memory directly, and data passed between them gets pickled. Use them for CPU-bound work: image processing, compression, number crunching.
9df1a05865:
asyncio takes a third path: one thread, one process, but many tasks that cooperate. Each task runs until it hits an await, which means "I'm waiting, run someone else." The event loop then switches to another task. There are no GIL fights, no process overhead, and no shared-memory races. It scales to thousands of concurrent waits.

The price: your code must be written in async style throughout, and one blocking call freezes the whole loop.
46f6ed3cfa: Eight network calls drop from 1.6s to 0.2s, because the waits overlap. The number crunching takes the same time with or without threads. The GIL lets only one thread compute at a time, so you paid the threading overhead for nothing. (Your exact timings will differ slightly run to run. What matters is the shape: big win versus no win.)
0275c31468:
Each tool has its common mistake.

  • With threads: mutating shared data without a lock. Two threads updating one counter can silently lose updates (a race condition).
  • With processes: spawning a process pool for a millisecond of work. The startup cost dwarfs the job.
  • With asyncio: calling a blocking function like time.sleep() or a synchronous HTTP library inside a coroutine. It freezes every task on the loop. The async equivalent of sleep is await asyncio.sleep().
7a160cb812: Sometimes you need none of them. If the program is fast enough sequentially, keep it sequential. Concurrency adds failure modes: races, deadlocks, tasks that never finish. Simple code you can reason about beats clever code you cannot.
f41c171ea8: Here is the mental model for asyncio in a few sentences. A coroutine is a function defined with async def that can pause itself. await is the pause button. It says: "suspend me until this slow thing finishes, and let other tasks run meanwhile." The event loop is the scheduler. It watches all paused tasks and wakes each one when its wait is over. asyncio.run() builds the loop, runs your top-level coroutine, and closes everything down.
b88535d060:
Three more terms for the example.

  • A Task wraps a coroutine so the loop can schedule it independently (asyncio.create_task).
  • asyncio.gather runs several coroutines concurrently and returns their results in order.
  • asyncio.wait_for sets a deadline. If the task is not done in time, it gets cancelled and TimeoutError is raised.

(Since Python 3.11, asyncio.TimeoutError is the builtin TimeoutError, so there's one name to catch.)
94ec072ed1: Read the output like the loop does. All three fetches start before any finishes. Each await asyncio.sleep hands control back, so the loop starts the next one. They finish in order of their delays (orders, stock, users). But gather returns results in the order you passed them. Total time is 0.5s, the longest wait, not the sum. That is the whole payoff of async I/O.
fc15eaae80:
Two exception details are worth keeping.

First, wait_for cancels the slow task. It does not keep running in the background. Cancellation is how you enforce deadlines: "answer in one second or I stop waiting."

Second, an exception inside a task surfaces when you await that task. If you never await it, the exception sits unretrieved and Python warns you at shutdown. A practical rule: every task you create gets awaited somewhere, with handling where it makes sense.
d45c468292: One more gather behavior for the road. By default, the first exception raised by any of the gathered coroutines propagates out of gather immediately, and the other results are lost. If you want every result including failures, pass return_exceptions=True. Exceptions then come back as values in the results list instead of being raised. (That is stdlib behavior, not style advice.)
717d9ae7fc: Async is sometimes the wrong tool. CPU-bound work gains nothing on one thread. A script with two sequential steps gains nothing but syntax. Mixing needs care too. If a library only offers blocking calls, run it in a thread from async code with asyncio.to_thread() rather than calling it directly. That keeps the loop responsive.
d5a92f091e: Performance work has an order of operations, and skipping steps is how people waste afternoons. First, think about the algorithm: how does the work grow as the input grows? Then measure to find where time actually goes. Then, and only then, optimize. The honest rule behind all of it: most speedups come from doing less work, not from doing the same work faster.
d2efcf17a5:
Big-O is the vocabulary for "how does the work grow." O(n) means doubling the input roughly doubles the work: one pass over the data. O(n²) means doubling the input quadruples the work: a loop inside a loop. The difference looks academic at n=10 and brutal at n=10,000.

Big-O describes growth, not seconds. An O(n²) algorithm can still win on tiny inputs. It is a thinking tool for choosing approaches, not a stopwatch.
77a7456501: That's a 1270x speedup with zero cleverness. The fast version just does less work. A set lookup is O(1) on average, so one pass replaces the nested scan. (Timings jitter run to run; the gap between the two approaches does not.)
5fb65e5da8:
Then comes the profiler. time.perf_counter() is the right clock for quick before/after timings. Unlike time.time(), it is monotonic and high-resolution.

cProfile answers the harder question: which function is slow. Read its table by the tottime column. That's the time spent in the function itself, excluding calls it makes. Here dupes_slow owns 0.286 of 0.287 seconds. No mystery, no guessing: the nested loop is the whole story.
8400a78f5f:
Performance work has its own common mistakes:

  • Optimizing before measuring. The slow part is rarely where you feel it is.
  • Micro-tuning the wrong function, such as saving microseconds in code that runs once.
  • Benchmarking sloppily. One run on a busy machine proves little. Compare approaches on the same machine, and distrust tiny differences.
a4602b70e5: So when should you optimize? Optimize the hot path the profiler identified, and only when the speed matters to someone: a user waiting, a bill growing, a batch missing its window. Code that runs in 0.000s, like the fast version above, is done. Readability wins every tie.
2d4a66155b: Never eval() untrusted input. eval takes a string and executes it as Python code. That is its entire job. Any part of that string might come from outside your program: a form field, a config file, an API response. If it does, treat it as hostile. An attacker can put anything in it, and eval will run it with your program's permissions.
767adf515f: Never unpickle untrusted data. pickle.loads rebuilds objects from bytes. Here is the mechanism. A pickled object can carry a __reduce__ method telling pickle which callable to invoke to reconstruct it. Pickle invokes it during loads(). So an attacker crafts bytes whose __reduce__ points at os.system or similar, and merely unpickling runs their command. The file extension does not matter; the bytes are the program.
b9368273e5: The payload string called a real OS function through eval. There was no exploit trickery, just what eval does. The pickle demo printed from inside loads(), before your program ever touched a result. Both prove the same point: these functions do not distinguish data from instructions.
3885e10e7e:
Two caveats are worth stating plainly.

ast.literal_eval is not a general expression evaluator. "{1,2} | {3}" fails because set union is an operation, not a literal. That refusal is the safety.

And json cannot represent every Python object: no tuples-as-tuples, no datetimes, no custom classes. That limitation is also the safety. When you need richer types across a boundary, define a schema and validate. Do not reach back for eval.
7995f8ad9f: When do these rules not apply? eval on a string your own code constructed from constants, in a REPL or a debugger, is fine. The danger is untrusted input, not the function. Pickle between two programs you wrote, over a channel you control, is the standard use. The rule is about trust boundaries. User input, uploaded files, network data, and third-party feeds are untrusted until validated.

d1cb95f3b2:
Solution 5:

  • (a) threads or asyncio. The work is waiting on the network, and the GIL is released during I/O waits, so 200 downloads overlap.
  • (b) multiprocessing. Thumbnail generation is pure CPU work. Threads would serialize on the GIL, while separate processes truly run in parallel.
  • (c) asyncio. 10,000 mostly-idle connections are thousands of concurrent waits on one thread. That's exactly what the event loop is built for, with none of the per-thread memory cost.
